receipts.first_text_witness: You're at Chipotle and you're doing the math on whether guacamole is actually happening today. Not whether you want it, you want it, but whether you can. You make $38,000 a year, which means you earn more than roughly a third of all full-time American workers. The guacamole is $2.75. The math is still tight. Now, picture someone else. Different city, same age, same hours in the work day, who booked a last-minute flight to Austin last Tuesday because tickets were cheap and she felt like going. Checked out, bought the ticket, didn't think about it again until she packed. Didn't do any math at all. These two people are not living different versions of the same life. They are living completely different lives. And here's the thing that should stop you cold. The gap between them isn't luck, and it isn't some massive salary difference. It's a specific, measurable threshold. Researchers actually have a name for it. My name is Nick and today we're going to find it. Before we talk about what different paychecks actually buy you, let's establish where everyone is standing cuz most people dramatically misread their position on the American income ladder, and that misreading costs them. The median household income in America right now is $83,730. That is not one high earner. That is the entire household. Everyone working under that roof combined. The median individual full-time worker earns around $62,000. So, when two people say, "We're doing fine. We make six figures together." they are describing a household income that is about average, not rich, not poor, just median. Pew Research puts roughly 30% of Americans in a low-income household, under $56,000 combined. The core middle class runs $75,000 to $125,000. Only about 10% of households crack $250,000. And here's the fact almost nobody in financial media bothers to mention 42.8% of American households now earn over $100,000. Sounds like a lot of comfortable people except when you run the actual monthly numbers which we are about to do in detail, you realize that $100,000 in Chicago is a completely different financial reality than $100,000 in Lubbock, Texas. SmartAsset ran the data. A $100,000 salary in Manhattan has the purchasing power of just $30,362 in real terms. $30,000. The same paycheck two different cities, two completely different lives. So, what we're really asking today isn't what is your salary say, it's a single question for every income level. At what point does money start working for you instead of the other way around? Let's find out.
